history: Gradual visual zigzags lasting 25 minutes followed by unilateral pulsating headache, nausea and photophobia. Similar episodes for years.
exam: Normal neurological examination between episodes.

tests.Headache history: At least five stereotyped headaches, 8–16 hours each; aura evolves over minutes.
tests.Neurological examination: No focal deficit, fever, or meningism.

clues: Gradual reversible visual aura preceding headache
why: Characteristic stereotyped migraine features; assess red flags before labeling primary headache.
plan: Screen for sudden-onset red flags; acute symptom relief and preventive discussion if frequent.

history: Bilateral pressing discomfort after long workdays, without vomiting or aura.
exam: Normal neurological examination.

tests.Headache history: Bilateral nonpulsating mild–moderate pain; physical activity does not worsen it.
tests.Neurological examination: No focal abnormalities or red flags.

clues: Bilateral pressing headache without migrainous features
why: Features favor tension-type rather than migraine; exclude secondary red flags.
plan: Discuss sleep, stress, analgesic overuse and appropriate symptomatic care.

chief: One side of face suddenly weak
history: Over 18 hours, difficulty closing right eye and smiling; no arm weakness or speech disturbance.
exam: Right upper and lower facial weakness including forehead; limbs normal.

tests.Cranial nerve examination: Right peripheral pattern of CN VII weakness; forehead involved.
tests.Glucose and focused assessment: No vesicles or other cranial nerve signs; assess alternate causes.

why: Peripheral facial nerve palsy; central causes and Ramsay Hunt require assessment.
differentials: Stroke; Ramsay Hunt syndrome; Lyme disease
plan: Protect cornea; prompt clinician assessment for corticosteroids and alternate causes.

history: Thumb, index and middle finger paresthesia wakes her; shaking hand helps.
exam: Median-distribution sensory symptoms, possible thenar weakness.

tests.Nerve conduction study: Median neuropathy at wrist with prolonged distal latency.
tests.Focused hand examination: Median distribution symptoms, positive provocative maneuver.

why: Entrapment at carpal tunnel is supported by clinical pattern and nerve conduction.
plan: Splinting, ergonomic assessment; consider specialist referral if weakness or persistent symptoms.

chief: Low mood and loss of interest
history: For 7 weeks, persistent depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, poor concentration and guilt, impairing work. No past mania.
exam: Psychomotor slowing; coherent thought, no psychosis.

tests.Structured clinical interview: Five or more depressive symptoms including depressed mood/anhedonia for over 2 weeks, with impairment.
tests.Safety and medical screen: Assess suicide risk, bipolar history, substances and medical mimics.

clues: Persistent anhedonia and mood symptoms with impairment
why: A major depressive episode is plausible after exclusion of mania, substance and medical explanations.
plan: Assess safety, discuss evidence-based psychotherapy and/or medication with a clinician.

history: Unexpected surges of palpitations, trembling and fear of dying; worries about more attacks for 2 months.
exam: Between attacks, examination unremarkable.

tests.Clinical interview: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks and persistent concern/behavior change over a month.
tests.Medical and substance review: Evaluate cardiac, thyroid, stimulant and other mimics.

clues: Unexpected recurrent panic attacks plus anticipatory anxiety
why: Persistent worry after attacks distinguishes disorder from isolated panic attacks.
plan: Rule out medical causes and discuss CBT with interoceptive exposure.

history: Excessive worry across finances, family and work most days for 9 months, with restlessness, tension and poor sleep.
exam: No psychosis or manic features.

tests.Clinical interview: Difficult-to-control multi-domain worry over 6 months, associated physical symptoms and impairment.
tests.Medical review: Assess caffeine, medication, thyroid and other contributors.

why: Time course and breadth of worry favor GAD.
plan: Discuss CBT, sleep interventions and treatment options.

history: Gradual asymmetric resting hand tremor, smaller handwriting and reduced arm swing.
exam: Bradykinesia with rigidity and resting tremor, asymmetric.

tests.Motor examination: Bradykinesia with decrement, unilateral rigidity and rest tremor.
tests.Medication and red-flag review: No dopamine-blocking drug exposure or early severe autonomic failure.

clues: Bradykinesia plus resting tremor and rigidity
why: Clinical parkinsonism with typical asymmetry supports Parkinson disease.
plan: Neurology review; functional goals, exercise and dopaminergic treatment discussion.

chief: Hands shake when holding a cup
history: Bilateral action tremor for 8 years, worse with stress, no slowness or stiffness.
exam: Postural and kinetic tremor without bradykinesia.

tests.Motor examination: Bilateral action tremor; no parkinsonian bradykinesia.
tests.Medication and thyroid review: Consider enhanced physiological tremor and thyroid disease.

why: Longstanding bilateral kinetic tremor is characteristic.
plan: Assess disability, triggers and treatment options.

history: Over 3 years repeats questions, misplaces objects and needs help with finances; gradual progression.
exam: Impaired delayed recall with limited cue benefit; daily functioning affected.

tests.Cognitive assessment: Episodic memory encoding/storage impairment and multidomain cognitive deficits.
tests.MRI brain and reversible-cause labs: Medial temporal atrophy; check B12, TSH and other contributors.

clues: Insidious progressive episodic-memory and functional decline
why: Pattern suggests Alzheimer clinical syndrome; biomarkers may be considered where appropriate.
differentials: Depression; vascular cognitive impairment; Lewy body dementia
plan: Comprehensive dementia assessment, support planning and discussion of appropriate therapies.

history: Stepwise cognitive decline with hypertension and prior infarcts; planning worse than recall.
exam: Executive slowing, mild left-sided weakness.

tests.MRI brain: Multiple strategic infarcts and extensive small-vessel disease.

why: Temporal relationship and imaging support vascular contribution.
plan: Optimize vascular risks and arrange multidisciplinary cognitive support.

history: Fluctuating attention, detailed visual hallucinations and dream enactment before major memory complaints.
exam: Parkinsonism and impaired visuospatial performance.

tests.Cognitive examination: Marked attention and visuospatial deficits with fluctuations.
tests.Sleep and movement history: Probable REM sleep behavior disorder and spontaneous parkinsonism.

clues: Fluctuations, hallucinations, REM sleep behavior and parkinsonism
why: Core clinical features suggest dementia with Lewy bodies.
differentials: Alzheimer disease; delirium; Parkinson disease dementia
plan: Specialist evaluation; caution with antipsychotic sensitivity.

history: Progressive disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and rigid food habits over 2 years.
exam: Executive dysfunction; memory relatively spared early.

tests.Behavioral and collateral interview: Progressive early behavioral disinhibition and loss of empathy.

clues: Early behavioral change over memory loss
why: Behavioral syndrome and frontotemporal pattern favor bvFTD.
plan: Specialist assessment, caregiver support and safety planning.

history: Painful monocular vision loss 9 months ago resolved; now subacute sensory and gait symptoms.
exam: Hyperreflexia, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, patchy sensory deficit.

tests.MRI brain and spine: Typical periventricular and spinal demyelinating lesions with dissemination in space; differing enhancement.
tests.CSF oligoclonal bands: CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands support inflammatory demyelination.

why: Clinical attacks plus MRI/CSF may meet contemporary diagnostic criteria after excluding mimics.
plan: Urgent specialist assessment for relapse and disease-modifying treatment.

history: Fluctuating ptosis and double vision, worse after activity, improves with rest.
exam: Fatigable ptosis and variable ocular weakness; normal sensation.
why: Neuromuscular junction dysfunction supported by antibody/electrophysiology.
differentials: Thyroid eye disease; botulism; cranial neuropathy
plan: Assess breathing and swallowing urgently if affected; specialist treatment.

history: One week after gastroenteritis, progressive symmetrical weakness and tingling over 4 days.
exam: Areflexia, symmetric ascending weakness.

tests.Lumbar puncture: Raised CSF protein with few cells may emerge after first week.

why: Acute inflammatory polyradiculoneuropathy; early CSF can be normal.
differentials: Spinal cord compression; myasthenia; tick paralysis
plan: Hospital assessment for respiratory and autonomic monitoring; IVIG or plasma exchange.

history: Repeated 60-second episodes of déjà vu, rising epigastric sensation and impaired awareness with lip smacking.
exam: Normal between events.

tests.EEG: Interictal temporal epileptiform discharges may be present.
tests.MRI epilepsy protocol: Possible mesial temporal sclerosis; normal imaging does not exclude epilepsy.

why: Semiology supports focal temporal seizures; EEG can support but not independently exclude.
plan: Seizure safety, specialist assessment and appropriate antiseizure treatment.

history: Abrupt aphasia and right arm weakness 45 minutes ago.
exam: Right face/arm weakness, aphasia; glucose normal.

tests.Noncontrast CT head: No intracranial hemorrhage on initial scan.
tests.CT angiography: Left middle cerebral artery large-vessel occlusion.

why: Time-critical vascular syndrome; imaging directs reperfusion eligibility.
differentials: Hypoglycemia; seizure with Todd paresis; migraine aura
plan: Activate emergency stroke pathway immediately; assess reperfusion options.

history: Abrupt language disturbance lasting 12 minutes, now completely resolved; vascular risk factors.
exam: Neurological examination normal now.

tests.Urgent vascular imaging: Carotid stenosis may be found; normal imaging does not rule out TIA.
tests.Brain MRI DWI: No acute infarction; absence of DWI lesion does not exclude TIA.

clues: Brief abrupt focal deficit without residual symptoms
why: Possible transient cerebral ischemia requires urgent stroke evaluation.
plan: Same-day emergency assessment and secondary prevention workup.

history: Head impact during sport, headache and slowed thinking, no focal deficit; no worsening red flags.
exam: Balance mildly impaired, GCS 15.

tests.Concussion symptom assessment: Headache, cognitive fog and light sensitivity after impact.
tests.Red flag and CT decision assessment: No high-risk signs; imaging decision uses validated clinical rules.

why: Clinical concussion diagnosis; routine CT does not diagnose concussion.
plan: Remove from play, monitor red flags and graded return to activity.

history: Intrusive fear of fire; checks stove repeatedly despite recognizing excessiveness, 2 hours daily.
exam: Anxious, intact reality testing.

tests.Structured symptom interview: Obsessions and compulsions are time-consuming and distressing.
tests.Differential and insight assessment: Thoughts intrusive; rituals aim to reduce anxiety, not delusion-driven.

why: Compulsions distinguish OCD from ordinary caution or generalized worry.
plan: Exposure and response prevention with clinician support; consider medication.

history: For 4 months has trauma-related intrusions, avoidance, hypervigilance and negative mood affecting daily life.
exam: Startles easily; oriented, no psychosis.

tests.Trauma-focused interview: Intrusions, avoidance, negative cognition/mood and arousal for over a month.
tests.Safety and comorbidity assessment: Assess current safety, depression, substance use and dissociation.

why: Duration and symptom clusters support PTSD; avoid unnecessary detailed trauma retelling.
plan: Offer trauma-focused evidence-based psychotherapy and supportive care.

chief: Sleeping 2 hours and making grand plans
history: One week of elevated/irritable mood, marked energy, pressured speech, impulsive spending and major impairment; prior depressive episodes.
exam: Grandiosity, distractibility and psychomotor activation.

tests.Longitudinal mood interview: Syndromal mania with impairment for at least a week or requiring hospitalization.
tests.Substance and medical assessment: Evaluate stimulants, thyroid disease and medication-induced symptoms.

clues: Manic episode with marked functional impairment
why: History of mania establishes bipolar I rather than unipolar depression.
plan: Assess risk and need for urgent psychiatric care; mood stabilization.

history: For 2 years fears negative judgment in class and social situations, avoids them, causing academic impairment.
exam: No panic outside feared social evaluation.

tests.Clinical interview: Persistent fear of scrutiny and avoidance for more than 6 months.
tests.Differential assessment: Evaluate autism, panic disorder and normative shyness.

why: Fear is tied to social scrutiny rather than unexpected attacks.
plan: CBT with graduated exposure; individualized treatment discussion.

history: Since primary school forgetful, loses materials, distractible at home and school; longstanding impairment.
exam: Normal neurological examination.

tests.Developmental and school collateral: Several inattentive symptoms before age 12 in at least two settings.
tests.Learning and mood evaluation: Assess sleep, anxiety, depression and learning disorder mimics.

why: Developmental pattern is required; attention difficulties alone are nonspecific.
plan: Multimodal supports and formal specialist evaluation.

history: Eight months of functional decline, persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations and disorganized speech; no sustained mood episode.
exam: Thought disorder, blunted affect and impaired functioning.

tests.Psychiatric longitudinal interview: Active psychotic symptoms with continuous disturbance over six months.
tests.Medical and substance screen: Exclude substance-induced, mood-related and neurological causes.

why: Time course and syndrome support schizophrenia after differential evaluation.
differentials: Schizophreniform disorder; bipolar psychosis; substance-induced psychosis
plan: Collaborative early psychosis service, safety assessment and treatment.

history: Persecutory beliefs began shortly after a prescribed stimulant dose increase; no previous psychotic history.
exam: Agitated and suspicious; vital signs require assessment.

tests.Medication timeline: Psychotic symptoms closely track stimulant exposure and improve after discontinuation.
tests.Substance and medical assessment: Evaluate other substances, delirium and underlying primary psychosis.

clues: Psychosis temporally linked to stimulant exposure
why: Medication temporal association strongly informs differential, but follow-up is necessary.
plan: Urgent safety assessment and prescriber-led medication review.

history: Years of psychosis with major depressive episodes occupying most illness duration; also hallucinations for 3 weeks without mood symptoms.
exam: Current depressed mood with delusional thinking.

tests.Detailed longitudinal timeline: At least two weeks of psychosis without a major mood episode; mood episodes present for majority of illness.
tests.Medical and substance evaluation: No substance or medical cause identified.

clues: Psychosis outside mood episodes plus predominant mood illness
why: Longitudinal proportion of mood episodes differentiates from schizophrenia or mood disorder with psychotic features.
differentials: Bipolar disorder with psychotic features; schizophrenia
plan: Specialist longitudinal assessment and individualized psychiatric treatment.

history: Acute fluctuating confusion after urinary infection and medication changes.
exam: Inattention, altered awareness, sleep-wake disturbance.

tests.Bedside attention testing: Unable to sustain attention; fluctuates across hours.
tests.Infection, metabolic and medication work: Fever, inflammatory markers and medication burden suggest precipitants.

why: Delirium is a medical emergency and differs from chronic dementia.
plan: Identify and treat cause, medication review and supportive nonpharmacological care.

history: Progressive gait initiation difficulty, cognitive slowing and urgency over a year.
exam: Magnetic broad-based gait, executive slowing.

tests.Large-volume lumbar tap assessment: Objective gait improvement after CSF removal may support shunt responsiveness.

why: Suggestive triad and imaging prompt specialist assessment; triad not specific.
differentials: Parkinson disease; Alzheimer disease; cervical myelopathy
plan: Refer for neurosurgical and neurological evaluation.

history: Progressive asymmetric hand weakness, then leg weakness over 10 months; no sensory complaints.
exam: Atrophy and fasciculations with brisk reflexes.

tests.EMG and nerve conduction: Active and chronic denervation in multiple body regions; sensory studies often preserved.
tests.MRI and mimic evaluation: No compressive structural explanation; exclude treatable mimics.

clues: Combined upper and lower motor neuron signs
why: Progressive motor dysfunction across regions suggests ALS after excluding mimics.
plan: Prompt multidisciplinary neuromuscular care, respiratory and nutrition assessment.

history: Months of hand dexterity loss and gait imbalance with neck stiffness.
exam: Hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign and impaired tandem gait.

tests.MRI cervical spine: Cervical canal stenosis with spinal cord compression.
tests.Neurological examination: Upper motor neuron signs below lesion; hand clumsiness.

why: Cord compression explains progressive myelopathic signs.
plan: Expedited spine specialist assessment; urgent if rapidly worsening.

history: Acute fever, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness; increasingly unwell.
exam: Fever, meningism and altered alertness.

tests.Blood cultures and initial labs: Inflammatory response; blood cultures obtained without delaying therapy.
tests.Lumbar puncture when safe: Neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis, low glucose and high protein.

why: Bacterial meningitis requires immediate action; imaging before LP only when indicated.
plan: Emergency antibiotics and supportive management without avoidable delay.

history: Thunderclap headache reaches maximal intensity in seconds while exercising; vomiting and neck pain.
exam: Photophobia, neck stiffness; may have normal focal exam.

tests.Urgent noncontrast CT: Subarachnoid blood may be visible; sensitivity depends on timing and conditions.
tests.Further vascular/CSF workup: CTA and/or LP when indicated if CT negative and suspicion persists.

why: Potential aneurysmal hemorrhage is a time-critical emergency.
plan: Emergency neurovascular evaluation and stabilization.

history: Poor nutrition and heavy alcohol use, recent vomiting; new confusion and gait imbalance.
exam: Ataxia, nystagmus and disorientation.

tests.Clinical risk assessment: Malnutrition risk with encephalopathy and oculomotor/gait signs.
tests.MRI brain: May show mammillary body or thalamic abnormalities; normal MRI does not exclude.

clues: Ataxia, eye signs and confusion with nutritional risk
why: Clinical suspicion requires immediate thiamine; full triad often absent.
plan: Give urgent parenteral thiamine per clinical protocol and address nutrition.

history: Months of tingling, reduced vibration sense and difficulty walking in darkness.
exam: Loss of proprioception, sensory ataxia and brisk knee reflexes.

tests.Serum B12 and MMA: Low B12 with elevated methylmalonic acid supports deficiency.
tests.Spinal MRI: Possible posterior column T2 signal changes.

clues: Posterior column dysfunction with B12 deficiency
why: Subacute combined degeneration can cause mixed sensory and pyramidal findings.
plan: Prompt B12 replacement and evaluation of underlying cause.

history: Weakness fluctuates and is worse under observation; symptoms are real and disabling.
exam: Positive Hoover sign with internal inconsistency; no matching structural pattern.

tests.Focused positive-sign examination: Hoover sign demonstrates preserved automatic hip extension despite impaired voluntary effort.
tests.Targeted investigations: Tests guided by red flags; no evidence of another explanatory lesion.

why: FND is diagnosed using positive clinical features, not simply normal scans.
plan: Explain diagnosis respectfully; specialized physiotherapy and psychological support as indicated.

history: Two weeks of new psychosis, memory deficits, seizures and abnormal movements.
exam: Fluctuating consciousness and orofacial dyskinesias.

tests.CSF and neuronal antibodies: CSF anti-GluN1 IgG positive; inflammatory CSF may be present.
tests.EEG and MRI: EEG diffuse slowing; MRI can be normal or nonspecific.

why: Combined encephalopathy, seizures, dyskinesias and antibody support anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
differentials: Primary psychosis; HSV encephalitis; toxic-metabolic causes
plan: Emergency neurology care, infectious exclusion, tumor screening and immunotherapy.

history: Recurrent severe optic neuritis and prolonged spinal cord symptoms with bladder dysfunction.
exam: Bilateral visual impairment and spastic paraparesis.

tests.MRI spinal cord: Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning three or more vertebral segments.

clues: Severe optic neuritis with longitudinally extensive myelitis
why: AQP4-IgG with compatible core clinical syndrome supports NMOSD.
plan: Urgent relapse treatment and long-term specialist immunotherapy.

history: Weeks to months of cognitive decline, gait ataxia and myoclonus.
exam: Multidomain deficits, startle myoclonus.

tests.MRI brain DWI: Cortical ribboning and/or basal ganglia restricted diffusion.
tests.CSF RT-QuIC: Positive prion seeding assay supports probable prion disease.

clues: Rapid dementia with myoclonus and characteristic testing
why: Rapidly progressive syndrome demands evaluation for treatable mimics.
plan: Urgent specialist investigation and supportive care; evaluate reversible causes.

history: Early unexplained falls, axial rigidity and difficulty looking downward.
exam: Slow vertical saccades, supranuclear gaze palsy, postural instability.

tests.Ocular motor examination: Impaired vertical saccades and supranuclear gaze limitation.
tests.MRI brain: Midbrain atrophy may be present but not diagnostic alone.

clues: Early falls plus vertical gaze abnormality
why: Atypical parkinsonism with oculomotor deficits suggests PSP.
plan: Movement-disorder specialist assessment and falls/swallowing support.

history: Rapidly progressive parkinsonism with early urinary dysfunction and severe orthostatic hypotension.
exam: Rigidity, bradykinesia and substantial blood pressure drop standing.

tests.MRI brain: Possible putaminal or pontocerebellar changes; diagnosis remains clinical.

clues: Early prominent autonomic failure plus parkinsonism
why: Suggests MSA rather than typical Parkinson disease.
differentials: Parkinson disease; pure autonomic failure; DLB
plan: Specialist autonomic and movement care; prevent falls and manage symptoms.

history: Progressive choreiform movements, executive difficulties and mood changes; affected parent.
exam: Chorea, motor impersistence and executive dysfunction.

tests.Cognitive and psychiatric evaluation: Executive and behavioral impairment; assess safety.

clues: Autosomal dominant family history with chorea
why: Typical triad and genetic confirmation support Huntington disease.
plan: Genetic counseling and multidisciplinary symptom management.

history: Daily irresistible sleep episodes, emotion-triggered knee buckling with preserved awareness, sleep paralysis.
exam: Normal between episodes.

tests.Polysomnography then MSLT: Mean sleep latency ≤8 minutes and at least two sleep-onset REM periods in appropriate conditions.
tests.Sleep and medication review: Exclude insufficient sleep, sleep apnea and REM-suppressing medications.

why: Cataplexy and appropriate sleep testing support narcolepsy type 1.
plan: Sleep specialist review and safety counseling for driving.

history: New unilateral temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication; transient visual blurring.
exam: Tender temporal artery; possible visual deficit.

tests.ESR, CRP and CBC: Inflammatory markers elevated, but normal results do not completely exclude.
tests.Temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy: Halo sign or histologic arteritis supports diagnosis.

clues: New headache with jaw claudication and visual threat
why: Suspected GCA is a vision-threatening emergency.
plan: Urgent same-day assessment and glucocorticoids when strongly suspected.

history: Progressive loss of word comprehension and object naming, fluent speech, relatively preserved episodic memory early.
exam: Impaired single-word comprehension and semantic knowledge.

tests.Language neuropsychology: Severe confrontation naming and single-word comprehension deficits.
tests.MRI brain: Predominantly anterior temporal atrophy, often left greater than right.

clues: Progressive semantic loss with anterior temporal atrophy
why: Language-led neurodegeneration consistent with semantic-variant PPA.
plan: Specialist language and dementia assessment; speech-language support.

history: Longstanding pattern since adolescence of unstable relationships, identity disturbance, impulsivity and fear of abandonment across contexts.
exam: Affect rapidly reactive; evaluate self-harm risk without assumptions.

tests.Longitudinal structured interview: Pervasive enduring pattern across situations, not limited to mood episodes.
tests.Differential and safety assessment: Assess trauma, bipolar episodes, substance use and self-harm risk.

clues: Persistent cross-context interpersonal and identity instability
why: Personality pattern must be enduring; avoid diagnosis from a single crisis.
plan: Collaborative formulation and evidence-based psychotherapy such as DBT.

history: Persistent restriction with intense fear of weight gain and body image disturbance; low weight for developmental context.
exam: Bradycardia and orthostatic symptoms raise medical concern.

tests.Eating-disorder interview: Restriction, fear of weight gain and body image disturbance with significantly low weight.
tests.Medical stability evaluation: Vitals, ECG, electrolytes and refeeding risk assessment.

why: Diagnosis requires assessment of nutrition, cognitions and medical severity.
plan: Prompt multidisciplinary treatment; urgent medical assessment if unstable.

history: Multiple motor tics and vocal tics waxing and waning for over 18 months, onset age 8.
exam: Brief suppressible movements and throat clearing.

tests.Developmental tic history: Multiple motor and at least one vocal tic present over a year with childhood onset.
tests.Comorbidity assessment: Evaluate ADHD, OCD and functional impairment.

clues: Childhood motor and vocal tics persisting over a year
why: Clinical diagnostic criteria distinguish Tourette from transient tic disorders.
plan: Psychoeducation and CBIT if tics cause impairment.

history: Chronic pain with disproportionate time, anxiety and repeated checking; symptoms genuinely experienced.
exam: Exam and investigations guided by symptoms, not automatically assumed normal.

tests.Clinical assessment: Persistent excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviors related to distressing somatic symptoms.
tests.Medical review: Appropriate evaluation for concurrent physical conditions.

why: Presence of a medical illness does not exclude this diagnosis; symptoms are not fabricated.
differentials: Illness anxiety disorder; chronic pain with adaptive coping
plan: Validate symptoms, coordinated care and CBT-based approaches.

history: Subacute progressive headache and new seizure after recent pregnancy; papilledema.
exam: Possible focal deficit and raised intracranial pressure signs.
why: Venous imaging is required; standard noncontrast CT can miss CVST.
plan: Emergency specialist assessment and anticoagulation evaluation.

history: Progressive dystonia, tremor, psychiatric symptoms and abnormal liver enzymes.
exam: Dysarthria, dystonia and possible corneal rings.

tests.Ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urine copper: Low ceruloplasmin and elevated urine copper support diagnosis but require interpretation.
tests.Slit-lamp and liver evaluation: Kayser–Fleischer rings and hepatic involvement may be present.

clues: Young-onset movement disorder with liver findings
why: Treatable copper metabolism disorder requires comprehensive diagnostic criteria.
plan: Urgent hepatology/neurology care and copper-directed therapy.
